newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - German FDP confident of tax compromise.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - German FDP confident of tax compromise.

text.p: The parliamentary leader of Germany's Free Democrats (FDP), the pro-business junior partner in Chancellor Helmut Kohl's coalition, said on Wednesday that the chances for compromise over tax reform with the opposition were improving.

Kohl's coalition of Christian Democrats (CDU/CSU) and Free Democrats plan to pass tax legislation for 1998 and 1999 in the lower house on Thursday, but the bills are expected to be blocked next month by the opposition-controlled upper house.
"I believe a compromise is conceivable," FDP parliamentary leader Hermann Otto Solms told reporters. "The Social Democrats have given in on a few points."

Ingrid Matthaeus-Maier, finance expert for the Social Democrats (SPD), told the business daily Handeslblatt there were several points on which a compromise could be reached, such as entry-level tax rates and the level of tax-free income.

But SPD proposals to fund some of their tax cut proposals by raising other taxes are unlikely to win support from the government coalition, itself divided over staunch FDP resistance to any tax hikes.

The SPD parliamentary group has approved its own draft bill that aims to lower supplementary wage costs by cutting social security payments by two percentage points. The payments include contributions to unemployment insurance, as well as health and pension insurance.
In order to pay for the cut in unit wage costs, the SPD has proposed raising petrol taxes by six pfennigs per litre.
Separately, parliamentary deputies from Kohl's ruling coalition approved changes to the government's tax reform bill, virtually ensuring its passage in the lower house.
The changes agreed by the coalition include a number of last-minute modifications to corporate tax rules that have sparked a storm of protest from German industry.
"Ninety percent of companies are not affected by the new rules," said Solms in defence of the measures.

The most controversial changes are a new rule making it more difficult for companies to reduce their tax liability by carrying forward losses from previous years and the introduction of a tax on hidden reserves for power utilities.
Hans-Olaf Henkel, president of the Federation of German Industry, told Reuters the changes were a populist move that would make it harder for German companies to compete.
"If this package is implemented things will get much worse," he said.

He said the changes would particularly hit companies that have counted on being able to carry forward losses, such as those who invested in eastern Germany, foreign investors and new companies who tend to run up losses in the start of operations.

"We are very disappointed and deeply worried about how things are developing," he said. "It seems the ruling coalition is in a battle with the opposition to see who can put forward the most populistic tax proposal."
Meanwhile, the SPD continued to gnaw at Finance Minister Theo Waigel's budget plans, saying the government had already run up a deficit that exceeded its targets for the full year.
"The beeline drive of Kohl and Waigel straight into the budget hole is continuing unabated and has hit a new negative record," said Karl Diller, an SPD parliamentary finance expert.
He said that at the end of May, the federal deficit was already 53.4 billion marks ($30.9 billion), compared to a projected deficit for the year of 53.3 billion.
The finance ministry dismissed SPD plans to file a complaint with the Constitutional Court alleging Bonn's 1996 budget violated the constitution by exceeding public investment.
While acknowleging that its 1996 budget deficit was higher than public investment that year, the ministry said in a statement that the SPD's claim was not justified.

Irmgard Karwatzki, state secretary in the finance ministry, said prevailing legal opinion agreed that the constitution forbids planning a deficit above the level of investment, but not actually running a deficit above the level of investment.
"Therefore the 1996 federal budget conforms to the constitution. The SPD complaint will not be successful," she said in a statement.
-- Bonn Newsroom, 49 228 26097 150 ($ = 1.725 German Marks)
